newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - "Bruised" energy swaps bank on deregulation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - "Bruised" energy swaps bank on deregulation.

text.p: Deregulation and liberalisation of the natural gas and electricity markets will continue to spark energy derivatives trading on both sides of the Atlantic, industry players told a conference on Monday.

Swaps trading in natural gas and electricity will also get a boost from the success of futures contracts for those markets -- part of their so-called "commoditization" -- with some predicting the New York Mercantile Exchange's electricity futures could become the biggest U.S. energy contract.

But the black eye suffered by the industry as a result of several futures scandals in the last five years was still a peripheral topic at the conference sponsored by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association.
The International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) launched a natural gas contract on January 31 and NYMEX electricity futures began trading last year.
Some said they were hesitant to use the "D" word in marketing their derivatives to clients, particularly because of the sound it makes to a company's shareholders.
"I think that with some clients I would be more hesitant to say let's do a 'derivative' transaction," said Shannon Burchett, senior vice president at a large U.S. energy company.

"It's probably a better image to say a financial solution may be appropriate in this situation," he said. "People are a little paranoid about being the one who does a complex derivative transaction...It's just a matter of terminology."

He also warned that some utilities may not be prepared for using derivatives in the U.S. electricity market, which he estimated at $207 billion a year, dwarfing the next largest crude market at $87.88 billion.
"I think the industrials are probably a notch up the curve on risk management control," he said.

"It may not be the case for the utilities and they're going to be the big users...I don't want to be predicting disaster but I think it is a big potential that one has to be concerned about from a risk control standpoint."

But deregulation in Europe and the U.S., high price volatility, and a natural gas pipeline to join the U.K. and the rest of Europe in October 1998, will all increase cash market trading and inevitably swaps, they said.

"It gives it a bit of a bruise certainly, but I think in the long term it is healthy for the swaps industry because it makes people focus on the controls that are necessary in the management of these risks," said Jay Fitzgerald, vice president at Enron Capital and Trade Resources.
But he said energy swaps in Europe in the long run would be a "high growth market" capitalizing on European Union initiatives on electricity and gas.

"The EU will be providing that same type of oversight (as state governments in the U.S.), but I think EU will give its member states a lot more leeway in how they adopt initiatives," which will help trading in the physical and over-the-counter markets, he said.

The U.K. gas market has shown very few derivatives transactions but the volatile prices, the new natural gas pipeline and the unlocking of existing supply contracts will boost cash trading, and then swaps, said Mahul Raval, a broker at PVM Oil Futures Limited.

"Volatility will lead to a floating price system and more sophisticated price risk management including use of derivatives," he said. Despite these optimistic forecasts, they acknowledged it was difficult to put an exact dollar amount on the energy swaps market, and therefore difficult to predict specific growth rates.
